desc:
perm is a permutation of 0..n-1. For an index i, define f(i) = perm[i], and let fk(i) be the result of applying f to i exactly k times (f0(i) = i).

Return the array res of length n with res[i] = fk(i). Note that k can be as large as 109, so simulating every step is too slow.

Example: perm = [1, 2, 0, 4, 3], k = 2 returns [2, 0, 1, 3, 4].
hints: Repeating the step k times for every index costs O(n · k), far too slow when k is large.
A permutation splits indices into cycles. Inside a cycle of length L, going k steps is the same as going k mod L steps.
Walk each cycle once and store its indices in a list cyc. The element at list position j ends up at cyc[(j + k) % L].
editorial: Follow i -> perm[i] to extract every cycle as a list in walking order: cyc[0], cyc[1] = perm[cyc[0]], .... After k applications, the index at position j of its cycle has moved to position (j + k) mod L, because completing a full loop of L steps changes nothing.

So for each cycle set res[cyc[j]] = cyc[(j + k) % L]. Each index belongs to exactly one cycle, so the total work is O(n) regardless of k. Repeated squaring of the permutation also works (O(n log k)) but needs more code.
solution:
def applyPermutation(perm, k):
    n = len(perm)
    res = [0] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    for i in range(n):
        if not seen[i]:
            cyc = []
            j = i
            while not seen[j]:
                seen[j] = True
                cyc.append(j)
                j = perm[j]
            L = len(cyc)
            shift = k % L
            for pos, idx in enumerate(cyc):
                res[idx] = cyc[(pos + shift) % L]
    return res
